items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-06-14
items.q: This man Sue Sean gave out articles that Tom Brown was a great man.

ctx.x: This is a Negro who had never been recognized, invented by Alan Lomax. With a few jugs of wine and a couple of needles, furnished by the doctors in New Orleans. He was a set up and tell the history of jazz. A Negro who had never been recognized. Saw what the world broke. Nobody ever listened to him, but Alan Lomax happened to be one of the clique. That is Marshall Starnes, I can name him, for I don't have the list of them. They got a whole bunch of them. They live by piracy and lies. That's all they ever did in…

Well, I don't really think I can, Mr. Rocker. I think that I think I've covered everything. After all, I'm one of those people that just like listening to jazz music. I haven't any sort of first-hand knowledge of what really went on. I wasn't around. I wasn't even born when the first records were made, when jazz was created. But I've done the best I can to catch up with it since. And I was determined to come to the second time I came to New Orleans. I was determined to meet you and to see your files and to have a…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-16
items.q: He came down to New Orleans and he sold them a bill of goods to Myra Menville and Dr. Sushant.

ctx.x: You don't see anything in front of me that I take notes from, only just from what comes to my mind. That's why I don't have it in chronological order. I can only tell you what I can think of at the time. Maybe my talk may be gobbled up a little bit, that I might put this one before the other one, the other one before the other one. But I am telling you the true facts of this music. It was in Chicago where I changed the rhythm. They had a certain dance team. They were doing a castle walk. And up in the north,…
Can you hold it a second?

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-02
items.q: When he got mixed with Sushon, that all came up later, about the numbers that he had composed.

ctx.x: I have a record of Virginia Blues by the Louisiana Five in which they play the third strain of Skeleton Jangle as a part of the tune. It's signed, uh, Sincerely Yours, Don Fowler. Is there anything else you want to read?

You know, that's all. Not only the Louisiana Five, but everybody. It was a field lead from the all steel music and different things out the original Dixieland jazz band. Now they say these Negroes didn't hear these records. Joe heard them. If this man heard them, Joe Oliver heard them. Because Joe, in his thing, that's what he bases his rhythm on. Because he didn't know no better. He was just a Negro that didn't know no better. Like these even white crumbs who's supposed to be historians around New Orleans. They…

The letter here from... Let me see. I'll give you the full letterhead. It's a letter from Marshall W. Stearns. Yale Hot Club, 6th Linwood Place, New Haven, Connecticut. M. W. Stearns, President. Charter Unit of the UHCA. January the 11th, 1937, Mr. D.J. La Rocca, Earl Theater, Washington, D.C. Dear Nick, I have all your records from Liberty Stable Blues to the recent disc. I like the earlier ones better. Between you and me, our last argument should furnish you with plenty of publicity. I do think, however, that…

They may criticize me, but I have it here in the records where I got them. Now we'll take the fidgety feet. What would that remind you of? These men wouldn't know, but I am the man who composed it. I know. In my early days when I'd hear the drum go, boom, boom. That is the rhythm of that introduction. Now we come to the other part.
